title: Check if a number is prime (no factors other than 1 and itself — loop from 2 to sqrt(n)).
shortTitle: Check if a Number is Prime

s1_definition.profdef: A prime number is an integer greater than one that has no positive divisors other than one and itself. To test primality efficiently you only need to check for a divisor from two up to the square root of the number, because if a number has a factor larger than its square root it must also have a matching factor smaller than the square root. This reduces the work from linear to square-root time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India generating special indivisible token numbers for secure transactions, where a token is valid only if it cannot be split evenly into smaller equal groups except the trivial ones. Checking a token is like trying to divide a pile of coins into equal stacks of two, three, four, and so on. If no stack size from two upward divides the pile evenly, the pile is indivisible, that is prime. Cleverly, you only need to try stack sizes up to the square root of the pile, because any larger divisor would pair with a smaller one you already tried.
s1_definition.oneliner: A prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself, and you only need to test divisors up to its square root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A prime number is an integer greater than one that has no positive divisors other than one and itself. To test primality efficiently you only need to check for a divisor from two up to the square root of the number, because if a number has a factor larger than its square root it must also have a matching factor smaller than the square root. This reduces the work from linear to square-root time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India generating special indivisible token numbers for secure transactions, where a token is valid only if it cannot be split evenly into smaller equal groups except the trivial ones. Checking a token is like trying to divide a pile of coins into equal stacks of two, three, four, and so on. If no stack size from two upward divides the pile evenly, the pile is indivisible, that is prime. Cleverly, you only need to try stack sizes up to the square root of the pile, because any larger divisor would pair with a smaller one you already tried.

**One line to remember:** A prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself, and you only need to test divisors up to its square root.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive primality test divides the number by every integer from two up to n minus one, which is linear time. The key optimisation is to stop at the square root of n. The reason is mathematical: divisors come in pairs that multiply to n, and in each pair one member is at most the square root and the other at least the square root. So if there is no divisor up to the square root, there is none at all.

The efficient loop is `for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) if (n % i == 0) return false;`. Writing the condition as `i * i <= n` avoids computing a floating-point square root and keeps everything in integers, which is both faster and free of rounding errors. If the loop finishes with no divisor found, the number is prime. Before the loop we handle the small cases: numbers less than two are not prime, and two is the only even prime.

A further optimisation checks two separately and then only tests odd divisors, since no even number above two can be prime, roughly halving the work. For very large numbers used in cryptography, trial division is too slow and probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin are used, which quickly decide primality with a negligible error chance.

A senior-level point is to be careful with overflow when writing `i * i <= n`; for very large n near the integer limit, the multiplication can overflow, so you use a long or compare `i <= n / i` instead. Primality underlies cryptography, including the RSA keys that secure banking communications, so understanding it connects a simple loop to real financial security.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India issues special reference tokens for high-security transactions and, for a particular scheme, requires each token number to be prime so it has a clean indivisible property used downstream. We must validate whether a proposed token number is prime before issuing it. That is exactly a primality check.

Problem 2 — Tokens are validated at high volume, so the check must be efficient. The square-root optimisation reduces the work dramatically compared to testing every divisor, which keeps the issuing service fast even under load.

In our mini-project we build a `TokenValidator` with an efficient `isPrime` method using the square-root bound and odd-only divisor checks, plus a small helper that lists the primes in a range. The demo tests several candidate token numbers and logs whether each is prime, and lists the primes between one and thirty.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: candidate token numbers 1, 2, 17, 18, 97, 100, 7919, then list primes up to 30.

Step 1: For 1, it is less than two, so the method returns false immediately. One is not prime.

Step 2: For 2, it matches the special two case and returns true. For 18, it is even and not two, so it returns false immediately without any loop.

Step 3: For 17, it is odd and greater than two. We test odd divisors starting at three. Three does not divide seventeen, and the next odd divisor five already has five times five equals twenty-five which exceeds seventeen, so the loop stops. No divisor was found, so seventeen is prime.

Step 4: For 97, we test three, five, seven, nine; none divides it, and the next candidate eleven has eleven times eleven exceeding ninety-seven, so we stop. Ninety-seven is prime.

Step 5: For 100, it is even, so it returns false at once. For 7919, the loop tests odd divisors up to about eighty-nine; none divides it, so 7919 is confirmed prime, and notice we only did on the order of forty-odd checks rather than nearly eight thousand.

Step 6: The primesUpTo thirty call runs isPrime on each number from two to thirty and collects the primes, yielding the familiar list two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three, twenty-nine.

```
[2026-10-26 21:15:02] INFO    Token 1 is prime? false
[2026-10-26 21:15:02] INFO    Token 2 is prime? true
[2026-10-26 21:15:02] INFO    Token 17 is prime? true
[2026-10-26 21:15:02] INFO    Token 18 is prime? false
[2026-10-26 21:15:02] INFO    Token 97 is prime? true
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  isPrime(n):
    n < 2 ? ──yes──→ false
    n == 2 ? ──yes──→ true
    n even ? ──yes──→ false
    │
    ▼ test odd i = 3,5,7,... while i <= n/i
    n % i == 0 ? ──yes──→ false (divisor found)
    loop ends no divisor ──→ true (prime)

  example n=97: test 3,5,7,9 (10²=100>97 stop) → no divisor → PRIME
  only ~sqrt(n) checks instead of n checks
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A prime number is an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself. The naive way to test primality is to try dividing by every number from two up to n minus one, but the key optimisation I always apply is to stop at the square root of n. The reason is that divisors come in pairs that multiply to n, and in every pair one member is at most the square root and the other at least the square root, so if there is no divisor up to the square root there is none at all. That drops the work from linear to square-root time.

In code I handle the small cases first: numbers below two are not prime, two is the only even prime, and any other even number is immediately rejected. Then I loop over odd divisors only, starting at three, which roughly halves the work. I write the loop bound as i less than or equal to n divided by i rather than i times i less than or equal to n, because for very large n the multiplication can overflow, and the division form is overflow-safe.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate special secure reference tokens that must be prime for a downstream indivisibility property. Because tokens are validated at high volume, the square-root optimisation keeps the issuing service fast; for a number like seven thousand nine hundred nineteen I do only around forty checks instead of nearly eight thousand.

The senior-level point I connect it to is cryptography. Trial division is fine for moderate numbers, but the enormous primes used in RSA key generation, which secures banking communications, are far too large for it, so there we use probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin that decide primality quickly with a negligible error probability. So a humble loop that checks divisors up to a square root is the same idea that, scaled up with smarter algorithms, protects real financial transactions, which is why interviewers like this question as a bridge from basic control flow to real-world security.
